1.

introduction

[
1
]

The plaintiffs bring an action in defamation
claiming that the defendants are jointly liable for vilifying the plaintiffs.
The defamatory publications have a particular focus on Mr. Raoul Malak
saying that he engaged in money laundering, kickbacks, bribery, and other
criminal activity.

[
2
]

The plaintiffs plead that the defendants, in
2012:

commenced a campaign of vilification against the plaintiffs for the
predominant purpose of destroying, diminishing or undermining their reputation
and thereby: (i) eliminating them from contention for traffic control contracts
in British Columbia, Alberta and elsewhere; (ii) prejudicing their position
with existing and potential clients, financial institutions, professional
advisers and investors and others; and (iii) causing others to shun and avoid
the plaintiffs and to regard them with hatred, ridicule and contempt.

[
3
]

Prior to trial, the parties agreed that all
liability issues would be tried first, with issues respecting remedy heard
subsequently.

[
4
]

For the reasons that follow, the Court finds the
known defendants to be jointly liable for each of the defamatory websites,
blogs, YouTube videos, emails, and other internet publications. For Island
Traffic Services Ltd. (“Island Traffic”), the defamation arises after September 21,
2012.

[
5
]

Mr. Malak is the only individual plaintiff.
With respect to the reputation of the individual, the Supreme Court of Canada in

Hill v. Church of Scientology of Toronto
,
1995 CanLII 59 (SCC)
, [1995] 2 S.C.R. 1130 at para.
107

stated:

… to most
people, their good reputation is to be cherished above all. A good reputation
is closely related to the innate worthiness and dignity of the individual. …

[
6
]

The Court wishes to emphasize that the stings of
the defamatory publications, which include that Mr. Malak engaged in
bribery, kickbacks, money laundering, prostitution, and other criminal activity
are all unfounded. It is unfortunate, yet unavoidable, that I must repeat the
defamatory stings in these reasons in order for them to be properly considered.

[
7
]

In some of the publications, there are
references to various Members of the Legislative Assembly of our province.
There was no assertion or any evidence that any of these Members did not act
other than ethically and responsibly.

[
8
]

Similarly, reference is made to several current
municipal officials, business executives, and various employees of
organizations not engaged by the current proceedings. Again, there is no
assertion, nor any evidence that any of these individuals did not act other
than ethically and responsibly. The two exceptions are with respect to the past
actions of Mr. Martin Chambers and Mr. Brian Slobogian who Mr. Malak
knew and to whom reference is made in many of the defamatory publications.

2.

the key elements of a defamation action

[
9
]

The onus is on the plaintiffs to prove the key
elements of a defamation action.

[
10
]

In
Grant v. Torstar Corp
.,
2009 SCC 61
,
Chief Justice McLachlin, writing for the majority stated:

[28]      A plaintiff
in a defamation action is required to prove three things to obtain judgment and
an award of damages: (1) that the impugned words were defamatory, in the sense
that they would tend to lower the plaintiff’s reputation in the eyes of a
reasonable person; (2) that the words in fact referred to the plaintiff; and
(3) that the words were published, meaning that they were communicated to at
least one person other than the plaintiff. If these elements are established on
a balance of probabilities, falsity and damage are presumed, … The plaintiff is
not required to show that the defendant intended to do harm, or even that the
defendant was careless. The tort is thus one of strict liability.

3.

balance of probabilities

[
11
]

The civil standard of proof is that of a balance
of probabilities. In
F.H. v. McDougall
,
2008 SCC 53
, Justice Rothstein,
writing for the Court, made clear that this is the only civil standard of proof
at common law, and described what constitutes the balance of probabilities:

[41]      Since
Hanes v. Wawanesa Mutual
Insurance Co.
,
1963 CanLII 1 (SCC)
,
[1963]
S.C.R. 154
, at pp. 158-64, it has been clear that the criminal
standard is not to be applied to civil cases in Canada. The criminal standard
of proof beyond a reasonable doubt is linked to the presumption of innocence in
criminal trials …

[42]      By contrast, in civil cases, there
is no presumption of innocence. As explained by J. Sopinka, S. N. Lederman
and A. W. Bryant,
The Law of Evidence
(2nd ed. 1999), at p. 154:

Since society is
indifferent to whether the plaintiff or the defendant wins a particular civil
suit, it is unnecessary to protect against an erroneous result by requiring a
standard of proof higher than a balance of probabilities.

It is true that there may be serious
consequences to a finding of liability in a civil case that continue past the
end of the case. However, the civil case does not involve the government’s
power to penalize or take away the liberty of the individual.

[43]      An intermediate standard of proof
presents practical problems. As expressed by Rothstein, Centa and Adams,
at pp. 466–467:

As
well, suggesting that the standard of proof is “higher” than the “mere balance
of probabilities” inevitably leads one to inquire: what percentage of
probability must be met? This is unhelpful because while the concept of “51
percent probability”, or “more likely than not” can be understood by
decisionmakers, the concept of 60 percent or 70 percent probability cannot.

[44]      Put another way, it would seem
incongruous for a judge to conclude that it was more likely than not that an
event occurred, but not sufficiently likely to some unspecified standard and
therefore that it did not occur. As Lord Hoffman explained in
In re B
[(Children),

[2008] 3 W.L.R. 1, [2008] UKHL 35
] at para. 2:

If a
legal rule requires a fact to be proved (a “fact in issue”), a judge or jury
must decide whether or not it happened. There is no room for a finding that it
might have happened. The law operates a binary system in which the only values
are zero and one. The fact either happened or it did not. If the tribunal is
left in doubt, the doubt is resolved by a rule that one party or the other
carries the burden of proof. If the party who bears the burden of proof fails
to discharge it, a value of zero is returned and the fact is treated as not
having happened. If he does discharge it, a value of one is returned and the
fact is treated as having happened.

In my view, the only practical way in which
to reach a factual conclusion in a civil case is to decide whether it is more
likely than not that the event occurred.

[45]      To suggest that depending upon the
seriousness, the evidence in the civil case must be scrutinized with greater
care implies that in less serious cases the evidence need not be scrutinized
with such care. I think it is inappropriate to say that there are legally
recognized different levels of scrutiny of the evidence depending upon the
seriousness of the case. There is only one legal rule and that is that in all
cases, evidence must be scrutinized with care by the trial judge.

[46]      Similarly,
evidence must always be sufficiently clear, convincing and cogent to satisfy
the balance of probabilities test. But again, there is no objective standard to
measure sufficiency. In serious cases, like the present, judges may be faced
with evidence of events that are alleged to have occurred many years before,
where there is little other evidence than that of the plaintiff and defendant.
As difficult as the task may be, the judge must make a decision. If a
responsible judge finds for the plaintiff, it must be accepted that the
evidence was sufficiently clear, convincing and cogent to that judge that the
plaintiff satisfied the balance of probabilities test.

4.

Background

a)

Publications

[
12
]

Most of the publications involve an internet article.
The article evolved in some respects although its key salient stings remained. It
is styled in variations of “Ansan Traffic Group Exposed”, “Ansan Group and Raoul
Malak Uncovered”, or “Raoul Malak Uncovered”. In these reasons, any of the
versions will be referred to as the “Uncovered Article”. A copy of one version
of the article is attached to these reasons as Schedule “A”. Schedule “A” is
the version of the article set forth in the Third Amended Notice of Civil Claim
at paragraph 20. Its key variation from earlier versions is that it has a
further section referring to tax evasion.

[
13
]

A blog with the Uncovered Article was also
posted by a person using the pseudonym, “Jim Arthur”.

[
14
]

Some of the other publications involve a poem
first published in August 2012. A copy of the poem is attached to these
reasons as Schedule “B”. A YouTube video with the poem was also posted by a
person using the pseudonym “Jim Arthur”.

[
15
]

In addition, on or about September 27,
2012, a person using the pseudonym Jim Arthur emailed a letter to Premier C.
Clark and the Honourable R. Coleman regarding the then outstanding request for
proposals (“RFP”) and request for statements of qualifications (“RFSQ”) for
traffic control services by the British Columbia Hydro Power Authority (“BC
Hydro”). Contemporaneously, a blind copy of the email was sent to the
defendant, Mr. Trevor Paine, by Jim Arthur. A copy of the email is
attached as Schedule “C”. In these reasons I will refer to the BC Hydro
RFP/RFSQ as the BC Hydro RFP, unless otherwise noted.

[
16
]

Finally, on or about November 13, 2012, an
anonymous complaint was made to what is referred to as the Telus Corporation (“Telus”)
ethics line with “Follow-Up Notes” submitted on December 20, 2012. Contemporaneously,
the defendant, Mr. Remon Hanna testified that he was sent an email from
Jim Arthur containing the Follow-Up Notes. A copy of the complaint with the
Follow-Up Notes are attached to these reasons as Schedule “D”.

[
17
]

The defamatory publications are many and
occurred over many months in the context of commercial dealings, including
tenders for a large contract with B.C. Hydro and an existing contract involving
Telus which had been extended.

[
18
]

As will become apparent, most of the
publications were posted on the internet, sent as emails or forwarded as a shared
hyperlink. A key issue is whether one or more of the defendants were
responsible for the article, the poem, the September 27, 2012 email to
Premier C. Clark and the Honourable R. Coleman and the anonymous Telus ethics line
complaint.

[
19
]

The Uncovered Article is a “hit piece” targeting
Mr. Malak and the Ansan Group. For the most part, the article was posted
on a flotilla of domain names surrounding the corporate plaintiffs’ actual
domain names or using Mr. Malak’s name.

[
20
]

The plaintiffs’ actual domain names included:

<ansantraffic.com>;

<ansantraffic.ca>;

<ansantrafficcontrol.ca>;
and

<ansangroup.ca>.

[
21
]

The pleaded sister ship domain names, with the
defamatory statements, included:

<ansangroup.biz>;

<ansangroup.info>;

]

In addition to the foregoing domain names, the

<moneylaunderer.mobi>;

b)

Context

[
23
]

Mr. Raoul Malak is the key principal of Ansan
Traffic Group Ltd. and the other plaintiff corporations. He directly or
indirectly controls each of them (some with his spouse Ms. J. Chun). Other
than where necessary, I will refer to the corporate plaintiffs as the “Ansan
Group”.

[
24
]

Island Traffic was owned by Mr. Brian Litster
and Mr. Greg Smith until it was acquired by the Ansan Group on September 21,
2012, after negotiations which started earlier that month.

[
25
]

Mr. Malak and the corporate plaintiffs are
engaged in the business of providing traffic control services.

[
26
]

The defendant, Mr. Philip Jackman is the
key principal of the corporate defendant, Valley Traffic Systems Inc. (“VTS”).
VTS and the Ansan Group are competitors in the traffic control business in our
province.

[
27
]

Mr. Paine is the vice-president of finance
for VTS.

[
28
]

Mr. Hanna is a businessperson and was the
principal of Advanced Traffic Solutions Inc. (“Advanced Traffic”). In these
reasons I will refer to Mr. Hanna and Advanced Traffic as Mr. Hanna,
unless otherwise specifically noted. As described below, in 2012, Advanced
Traffic had no assets and no operations. Mr. Hanna was its sole
shareholder. Mr. Hanna also viewed his financial arrangement with VTS to
be with himself and not Advanced Traffic.

[
29
]

In the last half of 2010, Mr. Hanna had
worked with the Ansan Group (through Advanced Traffic) as a subcontractor
responsible for further subcontractors undertaking specific traffic control or flagging
assignments. Near the end of 2010, the Ansan Group terminated Advanced Traffic’s
services.

[
30
]

In early 2012, Mr. Hanna and VTS discussed
working together. An agreement was reached. On January 18, 2012, VTS and
Advanced Traffic entered into a confidentiality and non-solicitation agreement
in connection with preparing a tender for an anticipated BC Hydro RFP.

[
31
]

In April 2012, the Ansan Group and VTS
discussed the possible acquisition of VTS or its assets by the Ansan Group. However,
on May 1, 2012, the Ansan Group terminated further negotiations with an
email at 11:01 a.m.

[
32
]

Later that same day, at 3:30 p.m., Mr. Hanna
emailed to Mr. Jackman a list of lawsuits in which Mr. Malak or the
Ansan Group had been a party. Mr. Jackman then sent the list to Mr. Paine.

[
33
]

On August 29, 2012, BC Hydro formally
announced the BC Hydro RFP, seeking province-wide traffic control services.
Under the BC Hydro RFP, the winning bidder would provide the traffic control
services directly for the Lower Mainland and Vancouver Island. Other areas of
the province would be undertaken by sub-contractors which had been pre-approved,
engaging the need for the RFSQ. The final date for tenders to be submitted was October 5,
2012.

[
34
]

From early 2012, VTS had planned to submit a
tender under its name with Island Traffic and Mr. Hanna serving as
subcontractors. After the September 21, 2012 acquisition of Island Traffic
by the Ansan Group, Island Traffic was not a participant in the VTS tender
plans.

[
35
]

Under Mr. Hanna’s agreement with VTS, Mr. Hanna
would not receive any remuneration, compensation, or other financial benefit
(other than the use of some office space) in relation to the BC Hydro RFP unless
the VTS tender was accepted. The terms of remuneration were not documented
other than some scribbled notes prepared by Mr. Paine, which he did not
tell Mr. Hanna he had made. Mr. Paine’s notes were not produced for
trial, including on a redacted basis.

[
36
]

In 2012, VTS’s annual revenue was approximately
$15 million. In his testimony, Mr. Jackman confirmed that an estimate of
$7 million to $9 million overall annual revenue from a successful BC Hydro
tender was reasonable.

[
37
]

During 2012, VTS and Mr. Hanna were also
interested in securing work from Telus. Previously, on June 28, 2010,
Telus had announced that it had reached an agreement with Ansan Industries Ltd.
for all of Telus’s flagging needs in our province. The contract was stated to
be for two years (commencing July 1, 2010) with a possible third year
option.

[
38
]

If Mr. Hanna were to have obtained a
contract in conjunction with VTS from Telus, Mr. Hanna would have enjoyed
remuneration from VTS on a similar basis to the arrangement he had made with
respect to a successful BC Hydro tender.

[
39
]

On or about June 14, 2012, the Uncovered Article
was first posted on the internet.

[
40
]

On June 18, 2012, Mr. Jackman shared, using
Google Toolbar, the Uncovered Article with Ms. K. Shannon, a VTS employee.

[
41
]

On June 21, 2012, Mr. Jackman shared,
using Google Toolbar, the Uncovered Article with Mr. Litster and Mr. Smith.
He also emailed a link to Mr. W. Storie, the then manager of the by-law
department of the Township of Langley together with a short note (described
below). He also forwarded a “new link” he had received from Mr. Paine to
the Uncovered Article to Ms. N. Biernaczyk, an assistant business manager
of the union representing VTS’s employees. The new link was shown as posted by
Jim Arthur.

[
42
]

On June 22, 2012, Mr. Paine, on behalf
of VTS, emailed Telus asking about the status of its traffic control contract
with Ansan Industries Ltd. (the 2-year period was nearing its end). Mr. Paine
testified that he believed Mr. Hanna had suggested sending the email.

[
43
]

On June 26, 2012, Mr. B. Atchison, on
behalf of Telus, responded by email that Telus was pleased with the level of
service currently provided and did not see “putting out a new RFQ in the near
or mid-term of the existing contract”.

[
44
]

After receiving Mr. Atchison’s reply, Mr. Paine
forwarded it to Mr. Hanna, copying Mr. Litster, Mr. Smith, and Mr. Jackman.
Mr. Hanna’s one-word reply was “Prick!”

[
45
]

On or about August 6, 2012, the poem was
first posted on the internet. On August 7, 2012, Mr. Jackman emailed
the poem to Ms. D. Hibbs, Ms. T. Kanester, and Ms. D. Clark, all
of whom were VTS employees.

[
46
]

By a separate August 7, 2012 email, Mr. Jackman
sent the poem to Ms. G. Froescher and Mr. B. Jacobi, both of whom
were VTS employees.

[
47
]

On August 14, 2012, Mr. Jackman shared
a link to the Uncovered Article, using Google Toolbar, with Ms. T.
Kanester, Ms. S. Koper, and Ms. G. Froescher. Ms. Koper was also
a VTS employee. Later in the day, Mr. Jackman sent the link to Ms. K.
McCormick, who owns her own flagging company. He later emailed the link to Mr. D.
Unger, one of his friends.

[
48
]

As noted, on September 21, 2012, Ansan
Traffic Group Ltd. acquired Island Traffic. As of that date, Mr. Litster
and Mr. Smith became employees of the Ansan Group. Mr. Smith was an
Ansan Group employee for approximately six months. Mr. Litster is still an
employee with the Ansan Group, serving as a senior executive overseeing
operations.

[
49
]

On September 27, 2012, “Jim Arthur” wrote an
email to Premier C. Clark and the Honourable R. Coleman regarding the BC Hydro
RFP. Jim Arthur blind-copied the email to Mr. Paine. As noted, the September 27,
2012 email is attached as Schedule “C”.

[
50
]

On October 5, 2012, tenders for the BC
Hydro RFP closed without extension.

[
51
]

On October 29, 2012, “Jim Arthur” sent a
further email to Premier C. Clark and the Honourable R. Coleman.

[
52
]

On November 13, 2012, an anonymous written
complaint was made on the Telus ethics line regarding the Telus traffic control
contract. The complaint refers to the Ansan Group.

[
53
]

On December 14, 2012, Mr. Jackman, on
behalf of VTS, wrote to the Honourable R. Coleman to ask for his support for
VTS’s tender for the BC Hydro contract, which had yet to be awarded.

[
54
]

On December 20, 2012, Follow-Up Notes were added
anonymously to the original November 13, 2012 Telus ethics line complaint.
As noted, the full complaint is attached as Schedule “D”.

[
55
]

The same day, Mr. Hanna emailed Mr. Jackman
with the subject line, “FYI”. The email is described as “Follow-Up Notes” and
match the “Follow-ups” of the Telus ethics line complaint.

[
56
]

In January 2013, VTS started to receive
work from BC Hydro in apparent anticipation that the contract would be awarded
to VTS.

[
57
]

On or about February 27, 2013, the BC Hydro
contract was awarded to VTS.

c)

Mr. Raoul Malak’s background

[
58
]

In the plaintiffs’ Third Amended Notice of Civil
Claim, they plead (at para. 24):

24.       … the true
facts are as follows:

•

The plaintiff Malak is an honest, trustworthy,
competent, reliable, diligent, well-educated individual who enjoyed an
excellent reputation in his business and professional life before the
defendants embarked on their campaign of vilification.

•

Malak was raised by a middle class family in
Egypt and attended excellent schools in that country. He graduated from an
excellent-quality, private French-language high school in Cairo.

•

Malak did not seek employment immediately after
high school because of his plans to further his education in the United
Kingdom.

•

Malak went to the United Kingdom in order to
attend recognized English universities. At all times, he was lawfully in
England with the appropriate, lawful immigration status.

•

During the first part of his stay in the United
Kingdom, Malak attended the University of Liverpool for four years and obtained
a bachelor’s degree in languages.

•

Malak subsequently attended the University of
Manchester for one year and was awarded a Master’s degree in Hotel and Catering
Management.

•

After obtaining his Master’s degree, Malak was
hired by the Excelsior Hotel in Birmingham, England where he remained for five
years, rising to the position of General Manager and establishing a
well-deserved reputation for honesty, integrity and competence. Malak resigned
from the position voluntarily, in order to immigrate to Australia, which he did.

•

Malak has never been involved, directly or
indirectly, in any enterprise or activities relating to: (i)
prostitution; (ii) corruption; (iii) bribery; (iv) secret commissions or “kickbacks”;
(v) money laundering; (vi) tax evasion; (vii) loan sharking; (viii) fraud; (ix)
sex offences involving adults or children; (x) theft; (xi) embezzlement; or (x)
any other criminal or immoral activity in the United Kingdom, Canada or any
other country.

•

Malak was not guilty of any misconduct in relation
to the Granville Island Hotel, in which he at one time held a 20% interest. He
played no role in management and was not involved in any financial
decision-making, which was the responsibility of other persons.

•

Malak does not associate with criminals and did
not have a relationship with Martin Chambers as described in the Malicious
Article. Like many other innocent victims of Chambers, he entered into a
contract with Chambers (pursuant to which the latter owed Malak a large sum of
money) before Chambers’ true character and misconduct became known. When
Chambers failed to pay the money as required, Malak was compelled to file
lawsuits against Chambers and his companies in Alberta and British Columbia.
Malak’s relationship with Chambers was confrontational and there was never any
ongoing collaboration with Chambers or any other close business relationship.

•

Chambers did not put Malak on a stipend. From
time to time, Chambers periodically made payments owing to Malak pursuant to
the contract.

•

Malak was not involved with a “tear-down house”
in Richmond. The Richmond property is an excellent residence in an expensive
neighbourhood.

•

Malak did not use Asian dating sites. Malak did
not “
import
” his wife to Canada. He met and courted his wife in Canada
and they remain devoted to each other.

•

Ansan is a legitimate business and is not
involved in any way in money laundering or tax evasion.

•

Ansan has grown through acquisition but does not
intend and has never acted to become a monopoly.

•

Ansan received no money from Martin Chambers and
has never been involved with Chambers in any other manner.

•

Malak served on the British Columbia Board of
Parole. He was not appointed to the Federal Parole Board. He had no involvement
with the case of Brian Slobogian.

•

Slobogian was never the Chief of Finance of
Ansan. His brief employment with Ansan was terminated after several months when
Malak became aware that Slobogian was not knowledgeable in accounting matters.

•

Malak has not made “side deals” with Unions or
otherwise sought to bring harm to Unions or to their members.

•

Malak has never evaded taxes and has at all
times been scrupulous in accurately reporting his tax liabilities.

[
59
]

Mr. Malak’s testimony generally reflected
and served to prove generally the foregoing pleaded facts. Ms. Chun’s
testimony reflected an educated, intelligent person with no basis for the
defamatory assertion that she was a “mail order bride”.

[
60
]

In the plaintiff’s pleaded facts, there is
opinion regarding reputation which is not technically necessary. In defamation
law, a plaintiff’s good character and reputation are presumed. The onus is on
the defendant to show otherwise.

[
61
]

By 2012, Mr. Hanna did not trust Mr. Malak.
In 2010, Mr. Hanna had worked with the Ansan Group for about six months.
Litigation had resulted. It was his view that he had been cheated by Mr. Malak
in his dealings with him and the Ansan Group. I will address Mr. Hanna’s
defence of justification (truth) in greater detail below.

[
62
]

Mr. Litster and Mr. Smith each testified.
They had had very serious concerns about Mr. Malak’s business practices.
I accept Mr. Litster’s explanation that their past concerns regarding
the extension of the Telus contract were because they had “some misinformation
at the time”. As noted, Mr. Litster and Mr. Smith sold Island Traffic
to the Ansan Group in September 2012 and Mr. Litster continues to
work for the Ansan Group.

d)

Jim Arthur, Mike Flagger, Anonymous

[
63
]

The pseudonym, Jim Arthur, was used in
connection with many of the defamatory publications. The Uncovered Article was
shown as posted by Jim Arthur on or about June 18, 2012, as was a YouTube
video with the poem in August 2012. The September 27, 2012 email to
Premier C. Clark and the Honourable R. Coleman was shown as sent from Jim Arthur
<jimarthur042@gmail.com>.

[
64
]

As noted, the Telus ethics line complaint and “Follow-Up
Notes” were made anonymously. Mr. Hanna testified that Jim Arthur emailed
the Follow-Up Notes to him.

[
65
]

On September 19, 2012, Mr. Jackman was
also sent an email from a “Mike Flagger” with the subject line “new email”. The
email simply read “Here is the new email address”. Mr. Jackman does not
recall receiving it.

[
66
]

Shortly later on September 19, 2012, a
person using the pseudonym, Mike Flagger, sent an email to the District of
Maple Ridge from “Mike Flagger [mailto:
concernedflagger@gmail.com
]. The
email
directed the recipient to the defamatory website
www.ansangroup.com
which contained a version of the Uncovered Article.

[
67

a)

Assessing Credibility

[
68

In writing for our Court of Appeal in
Faryna
v. Chorny
(1951),
1951 CanLII 252 (BC CA)
, [1952] 2 D.L.R. 354 at 356–357 (C.A.), Justice O’Halloran
described the trial judge’s task of making findings of credibility:

If a trial Judge’s finding of credibility is
to depend solely on which person he thinks made the better appearance of
sincerity in the witness box, we are left with a purely arbitrary finding and
justice would then depend upon the best actors in the witness box. On
reflection it becomes almost axiomatic that the appearance of telling the truth
is but one of the elements that enter into the credibility of the evidence of a
witness. Opportunities for knowledge, powers of observation, judgment and memory,
ability to describe clearly what he has seen and heard, as well as other
factors, combine to produce what is called credibility, and cf.
Raymond v.
Bosanquet

(1919),
1919 CanLII 11 (SCC)
,
50
D.L.R. 560
at p. 566,
59 S.C.R.
452
at p. 460,
17 O.W.N.
295
. A witness by his manner may create a very unfavourable
impression of his truthfulness upon the trial Judge, and yet the surrounding
circumstances in the case may point decisively to the conclusion that he is
actually telling the truth. I am not referring to the comparatively
infrequent cases in which a witness is caught in a clumsy lie.

The credibility of interested witnesses,
particularly in cases of conflict of evidence, cannot be gauged solely by the
test of whether the personal demeanour of the particular witness carried
conviction of the truth. The test must reasonably subject his story to an
examination of its consistency with the probabilities that surround the
currently existing conditions. In short, the real test of the truth of the
story of a witness in such a case must be its harmony with the preponderance of
the probabilities which a practical and informed person would readily recognize
as reasonable in that place and in those conditions. Only thus can a Court
satisfactorily appraise the testimony of quick-minded, experienced and
confident witnesses, and of those shrewd persons adept in the half-lie and of
long and successful experience in combining skilful exaggeration with partial
suppression of the truth. Again a witness may testify what he sincerely
believes to be true, but he may be quite honestly mistaken. For a trial Judge
to say “I believe him because I judge him to be telling the truth”, is to
come to a conclusion on consideration of only half the problem. In truth it may
easily be self-direction of a dangerous kind.

The trial Judge
ought to go further and say that evidence of the witness he believes is in
accordance with the preponderance of probabilities in the case and, if his view
is to command confidence, also state his reasons for that conclusion. The law
does not clothe the trial Judge with a divine insight into the hearts and minds
of the witnesses. And a Court of Appeal must be satisfied that the trial Judge’s
finding of credibility is based not on one element only to the exclusion of
others, but is based on all the elements by which it can he tested in the
particular case.

[

iii)

September 27, 2012 email to Premier C.
Clark and the Honourable R. Coleman

[
161
]

With respect to the September 27, 2012 email to Premier C.
Clark and the Honourable R. Coleman, Mr. Paine acknowledges receiving a
blind copy of the email. As noted, the sender was shown to be Jim Arthur.

[
162
]

In context, the September 27, 2012 email was particularly
remarkable. The email dealt with the BC Hydro RFP. The tender process was to
close shortly, on October 5, 2012. The Ansan Group had acquired Island
Traffic about a week prior to the email. The email described Mr. Malak as “a
man with ties to organized crime”. The email also accused Mr. J. Standfield
(BC Hydro) of having an improper financial relationship with Mr. Malak. The
email had the appearance as having been written by a concerned “whistle-blower”.
The BC Hydro contract would be a financially significant contract for VTS.

[
163
]

In cross-examination, Mr. Paine acknowledged that he had read the
email. He also viewed Mr. Standfield as the person “handling the BC Hydro
traffic control relationship” (VTS was also dealing with two other BC Hydro
officials as part of the tendering process). Mr. Standfield’s position
with BC Hydro is stated as “Portfolio Lead Program/Strategy Services
Transmission & Distribution Procurement”.

[
164
]

Mr. Paine’s blind copy of the email from Jim Arthur does not
show Mr. Jackman (or Mr. Hanna) as being copied. Mr. Paine
confirmed that he could not tell from the email if anyone but himself had been
blind-copied.

[
165
]

Mr. Paine testified that he could not recall discussing the
email with Mr. Jackman, including asking if he knew who Jim Arthur
was. Mr. Jackman says he “very well could have been” told of the email by Mr. Paine.

[
166
]

I cannot accept that Mr. Paine would not have spoken to Mr. Jackman
regarding the blind copy of the September 27, 2012 email to Premier C.
Clark and the Honourable R. Coleman but for very unusual circumstances. Mr. Paine
was active in preparing the tender for the BC Hydro contract with the closing
of tenders about a week away. The email asked that Mr. Standfield be
removed “permanently from the procurement process”. Mr. Paine had met Mr. Standfield
in the summer of 2012 as part of the information meetings related to the BC
Hydro RFP.

[
167
]

The inference I draw is that Mr. Paine did not speak with Mr. Jackman
because he knew Jim Arthur was a pseudonym for Mr. Hanna. If Mr. Paine
had told Mr. Jackman of the September 27, 2012 email, it is also
implausible that neither has a specific recollection. From VTS’s perspective,
it was an exceptional email to the Premier and a Minister of our province.

[

As noted above, there are three key elements which must be proven by
the plaintiff in a defamation action. First, the impugned words must carry a
defamatory meaning, such that they would “tend to lower the plaintiff’s
reputation in the eyes of a reasonable person.” Second, the words must in fact
refer to the plaintiff. Finally, the words must have been published, meaning
they were “communicated to at least one person other than the plaintiff”:
Grant

at para 28.

[
240
]

Below, I will describe how each of these elements has been
proven by the plaintiff, on a balance of probabilities. I have considered
the defamatory materials separately. That said, many of the materials share
common stings.

a)

Defamatory Meaning

i)

Test

[
241
]

In
Lawson v. Baines
,
2012 BCCA 117
at
para
13
, Justice Hinkson (as he then was), writing for our Court of Appeal,
noted the three ways that defamatory meaning can be conveyed:

a)

If the literal meaning of the words complained of are defamatory;

b)

If the words complained of are not defamatory in their natural and
ordinary meaning, but their meaning based upon extrinsic circumstances unique
to certain readers (the “legal” or “true” innuendo meaning) is defamatory; or

c)

If the inferential meaning or impression left by the words
complained of is defamatory (the “false” or “popular” innuendo meaning).

[
242
]

In
Weaver v. Corcoran
,
2017 BCCA 160
,
Justice Dickson, writing for our Court of Appeal, stated:

[72]      Where
the literal meaning of words is in issue, it is unnecessary to go beyond the
words themselves to prove that they are defamatory. Where a claim is based on
the inferential meaning of words, the question is one of impression: what would
the ordinary person infer from the words in the context in which they were
used? Both literal and inferential defamatory meaning reside within the words,
as part of their natural and ordinary meaning. In contrast, where legal
innuendo is pleaded the impugned words take on defamatory meaning from outside
circumstances beyond general knowledge, but known to the recipient.

Where the person to whom the words are

,

Substantial truth
is the test.  “An allegedly defamatory statement is not actionable if it is
substantially true”.  “It is sufficient if the substance of the allegation is
justified.”  The defence applies if the words are true in substance and in
fact.  If the defence is pleaded to multiple imputations, the court must
consider whether the evidence is sufficient to prove that each of the
imputations is substantially true.

“A statement is
substantially true where the alleged defamatory statement is no more
ignominious in the mind of the average listener than a true statement would
have been.”  Minor inaccuracies are acceptable and will be ignored.
The literal truth of the precise statement made does not have to be
shown.  The law “overlooks minor inaccuracies and concentrates upon
substantial truth.”  The test is substantial, not literal, accuracy.
”A technically false statement may nonetheless be considered
substantially true if, viewed ‘through the eyes of the average reader,’ it
differs from the truth ‘only in insignificant details.’”  If the
defamatory charge is true in substance, it is immaterial that there are slight
inaccuracies in the details of the expression, or with respect to secondary
items of importance.

If a false
statement in the publication is immaterial to the gist or sting of the libel,
it does not render an otherwise true statement defamatory.

And further (at 10-56 to 10-57)

The test is “whether
the libel as published would have a different effect on the mind of the reader
from that which the pleaded truth would have produced.”  In other words,
does the publication make the plaintiff significantly worse off than a
literally true publication would have, or would the plaintiff have been exposed
to any more opprobrium if the publication had been free from error?  It
must be “so misleading that it produces a different effect on a reader’s mind
than would the truth”.  If “the truth is so near to the facts as published
that fine and shaded distinctions must be drawn and words pressed out of their
ordinary usage to sustain a charge of libel, no legal harm has been done.”

[Footnotes omitted]

11.

vicarious liability

a)

Test

[
311
]

In
Bazley v. Curry
,
1999 CanLII 692 (SCC)
, [1999] 2 S.C.R. 534, Justice McLachlin
(as she then was), writing for the Court, in relation to the vicarious
liability of an employer for the acts of an employee, among other principles,
stated (at para. 41):

(2)        The
fundamental question is whether the wrongful act is
sufficiently related

to conduct authorized by the employer to justify the imposition of vicarious
liability. Vicarious liability is generally appropriate where there is a
significant connection between the
creation or enhancement of a risk
and
the wrong that accrues therefrom, even if unrelated to the employer’s desires.
Where this is so, vicarious liability will serve the policy considerations of
provision of an adequate and just remedy and deterrence. Incidental connections
to the employment enterprise, like time and place (without more), will not
suffice. Once engaged in a particular business, it is fair that an employer be
made to pay the generally foreseeable costs of that business. In contrast, to
impose liability for costs unrelated to the risk would effectively make the
employer an involuntary insurer.

(3)        In
determining the sufficiency of the connection
between the employer’s
creation or enhancement of the risk
and the wrong complained of, subsidiary
factors may be considered. These may vary with the nature of the case. When
related to intentional torts, the relevant factors may include, but are not
limited to, the following:

(a)

the opportunity that the enterprise afforded the
employee to abuse his or her power;

(b)

the extent to which the wrongful act may have
furthered the employer’s aims (and hence be more likely to have been committed
by the employee);

(c)

the extent to which the wrongful act was related
to friction, confrontation or intimacy inherent in the employer’s enterprise;

(d)

the extent of power conferred on the employee in
relation to the victim;

(e)

the vulnerability of potential victims to
wrongful exercise of the employee’s power.

[Emphasis in
original.]

[
312
]

In
671122 Ontario Ltd. v. Sagaz Industries Canada Inc
.,

2001 SCC 59
, the Court stated that whether there is control over a worker is
key to determining the imposition of vicarious liability. The Court stated:

[34]      What is the difference between an
employee and an independent contractor and why should vicarious liability more
likely be imposed in the former case than in the latter? This question has been
the subject of much debate. The answer lies with the element of control that
the employer has over the direct tortfeasor (the worker). If the employer does
not control the activities of the worker, the policy justifications underlying
vicarious liability will not be satisfied. See [Robert Flannigan, Enterprise
control:
The servant-independent contractor distinction
(1987), 37
U.T.L.J. 25], at pp. 31-32:

This basis for vicarious liability discloses
a precise limitation on the scope of the doctrine. If the employer does not
control the activities of the worker it is clear that vicarious liability
should not be imposed, for then insulated risk-taking [by the employer] does
not occur. Only the worker, authorized to complete a task, could have affected
the probability of loss, for he alone had control in any respect. Thus, because
there is no mischief where employer control is absent, no remedy is required.

b)

Relationship with VTS

[

]

[

Mr. R.D.
McConchie submitted that if there were not an employer-employee relationship, Mr. Hanna
was either VTS’s agent or Mr. Hanna and VTS were in partnership.

[

]

I
am satisfied that VTS gave Mr. Hanna sufficient authority to represent VTS
in its dealings with BC Hydro for Mr. Hanna to be viewed as an agent. As
such, the policy objectives set forth in
Bazley
, albeit set in an
employer-employee relationship, are met. VTS also had the requisite control
over Mr. Hanna to warrant VTS’s vicarious liability. VTS controlled
whether Mr. Hanna made representations to BC Hydro on behalf of the team
with the tender under VTS’s name only.

[

]

In
Colonial
Mutual Life Assurance Society Ltd. v. Producers and Citizens Co-Operative
Assurance Company of Australia Ltd
.
(1931), 46 C.L.R. 41 (H.C. of A.)
, the
High Court of Australia considered whether an insurance company should be
vicariously liable for one of its canvassers.

[
317
]

In
Colonial
Mutual
, a

Mr. Ridley had worked as an insurance canvasser for
the plaintiff insurance company. He had been dismissed by the plaintiff and
subsequently came to work for the defendant insurance company. In seeking
business for the defendant, Mr. Ridley defamed the plaintiff.

[
318
]

Justice Dixon (as he then was) writing one of the majority
opinions stated at p. 50:

If the view be
right which I have already expressed, that the “agent” represented the
Company in soliciting proposals so that he was acting in right of the Company
with its authority, it follows that the Company in confiding to his judgment,
within the limits of relevance and of reasonableness, the choice of inducements
and arguments, authorized him on its behalf to address to prospective
proponents such observations as appeared to him appropriate. The undertaking
contained in his contract not to disparage other institutions is not a
limitation of his authority but a promise as to the manner of its exercise. In
these circumstances, I do not think it is any extension of principle to
hold the Company liable for the slanders which he thought proper to include in
his apparatus of persuasion.

[
319
]

I have noted Professor P.S. Atiyah’s observation regarding
Colonial
Mutual
in his book, Vicarious Liability in the Law of Torts (London:
Butterworth, 1967) at p. 109:

Here, therefore, the High Court,
although denying the existence of any general liability for agents, affirms
such liability where the agent is representing the principal in transactions
with others. The reasoning is not, however, entirely easy to follow, for
despite the express denial of any general rule the logic of the reasoning would
seem to require such a general principle wherever the independent contractor is
acting as the principal’s “representative” — which would seem to mean the same
thing as agent. …

[
320
]

In
Sweeney v. Boylan Nominees Pty Limited
, [2006] H.C.A.
19, the majority (Gleeson C.J., Gummow, Hayne, Heydon, and Crennan JJ.) of the
High Court of Australia commented on
Colonial Mutual
:

[21]
Colonial Mutual Life
must be understood against the background of the development of this
area of law by the assertion and application of conclusions whose ultimate
roots are found in analogies which are no longer apt (if they ever were). But
whatever may now be seen to be the imperfections in the ultimate roots of this
area of the law, the conclusion reached in
Colonial Mutual Life
fits
entirely within the explanation of vicarious liability identified by Pollock [
Essays
in Jurisprudence and Ethics
, (1882) at 122] and reflected in the subsequent
decisions of this Court culminating in
Scott
,
Hollis
and
Lepore
.

[22]
Colonial Mutual Life
establishes that if an independent contractor is engaged to solicit
the bringing about of legal relations between the principal who engages the contractor
and third parties, the principal will be held liable for slanders uttered to
persuade the third party to make an agreement with the principal. It is a
conclusion that depends directly upon the identification of the independent
contractor as the principal’s agent (properly so called) and the recognition
that the conduct of which complaint is made was conduct undertaken in the
course of, and for the purpose of, executing that agency.

[23]      Pollock identified the element
common to cases of vicarious liability as being that “a man has for his own
convenience brought about or maintained some state of things which in the
ordinary course of nature may work mischief to his neighbours”. Pollock further
concluded that where an employer conducted a business, and for that purpose
employed staff, the employer brought about a state of things in which, if care
was not taken, mischief would be done. But the liability to be imposed on the
employer was liability for the way in which the business (that is, the
employer’s

business) was conducted. Conduct of the business and the employee’s actions
in the course of employment in
that
business were the only state of
things which the employer created and for which the employer would be
responsible. Thus for Pollock, course of employment was not a limitation or an
otherwise more general liability of the employer; it was a necessary element of
the definition of the extent of liability.

[24]      The conclusion reached in
Colonial
Mutual Life
, that the party engaging an agent (albeit as an independent
contractor) to solicit for the creation of legal relationships between that
party and others is liable for the slanders uttered in the course of soliciting
proposals, stands wholly within the bounds of the explanations proffered by Pollock
for the liability of a master for the tortious acts of a servant. It stands
within those bounds because of the closeness of the connection between the
principal’s business and the conduct of the independent contractor for which it
is sought to make the principal liable. The relevant connection is established
by the combination of the engagement of the contractor as the agent of the
principal to bring about legal relations between the principal and third
parties, and the slander being uttered in the course of attempting to induce a
third party to enter legal relations with the principal

[Footnotes omitted.]

[
321
]

In my view, Dixon J.’s reasoning in
Colonial Mutual

reflects the guiding principles subsequently articulated by our Supreme Court
of Canada in
Bazley
and
Sagaz
:

a)

was the wrongful
act sufficiently related to conduct authorized? (
Bazley
);

b)

was there a
significant connection between the creation and enhancement of the risk and the
wrong that occurred therefrom (
Bazley
); and

c)

was there control over the activities undertaken? (
Sagaz
).

[
322
]

As
seen above, Justice McLachlin in
Bazley
suggested possible relevant
factors. I do not consider these factors as limited to an
employer-employee relationship because they reflect the implementation of the
policy underlying the imposition of vicarious liability.

Mr. Hanna

Mr. Jackman

Crookes
